Content: In the realm of problem-solving, isolating the variable of interest is the algebraic equivalent of looking at the same picture from a different perspective. When we are given a formula, it is usually solved for one specific variable — meaning that variable sits by itself on one side of the equal sign. However, isolating a different variable of interest means rearranging the entire mathematical structure so that new variable is solved for in the equation. In real-world scenarios, rearranging a formula can be very useful - for example, a physicist might alter an equation that calculates distance in order to isolate for time instead.

On the SAT exam, gaining the ability to isolate a variable of interest is a can save time on Algebra and Advanced Math problems. Certain problems might present a complex scientific or financial formula then ask: “Which of the following expresses `t` in terms of the other variables?” If we can recognize the task at hand, then we can ignore any extra details and identify the solution by rearranging the equation until the variable of interest is alone on one side of the equal sign.

To solve these problems effectively, we must master the mechanics of literal equations. A literal equation consists mostly or entirely of variables instead of actual values, such the density formula in physics `D=m/V`. When asked  to solve for a specific variable of interest in a literal equation, the strategy is to perform inverse operations. Because there are no numbers to simplify, our work lies in systematically reversing the operations surrounding the target variable by moving everything else to the opposite side of the equal sign. This “undoing” process follows the order of operations in reverse, so the acronym becomes SADMEP insterad of PEMDAS.

The key to doing this without making a mistake is treating all the other variables exactly like regular numbers. If the variable of interest is being multiplied by another variable `V`, then we should divide both sides by `V'. If the variable of interest is trapped inside a fraction's denominator, you multiply both sides by that denominator to move it to the numerator on the other side of the equation. In more complex equations, you may need to use the distributive property to break out a variable trapped in parentheses or use factoring to isolate variable that appears in multiple terms.
